prose: The TARDIS breathes. A living machine, warm and low and constant, the hum of it pressed right through the soles of your boots. The air tastes of hot metal and old copper, cut by the wet-chip-fat stink of the alley bleeding in from the doorway. Rain taps at the cobbles out there, orange under the streetlamp. The man — the one who looks about — has his hands buried in his coat pockets. He hasn't moved. He's just watching you. Not a stare, not a challenge. A waiting look, like he's already decided something and is leaving room for you to catch up. The ship thrums around you both, patient as stone.

input: I don't move toward the doors. I move toward him, and I make myself hold his eyes even though everything in me wants to look at the floor. "You said anywhere. Any-when." My voice comes out smaller than I mean it to. "You've been waiting three days for me to say it, so I'll say it. Twelfth of November, 2003. Bethnal Green Road, east London. Late afternoon, going dark." A breath. "I'm not going to do anything. I just want to see her. My mum. Karen. I was six and I barely remember her face except from photos, and I want to see her walk down a street for ten seconds with her own legs. That's all. I swear that's all." I already know how it sounds. "Is that allowed? The way you do this — is that a thing that's allowed?"
prose: I close the distance. A step, maybe two — not quite into his space but near enough that the warmth comes off him, near enough that the rain on my coat is the only cold thing between us. I hold his eyes. They don't waver. They don't flinch. He's already waiting for it, the thing I've been carrying since the alley, and the words come out smaller than I meant them to. Smaller and raw, like something I've been clenching in a fist for three days and have just opened my hand to show him. His face goes still. The animation drains out of him — that rapid-fire energy, the hands that talk on their own, gone. He's just a man in a brown suit with rain-light on his face, and he doesn't answer for a long moment. The TARDIS hums. The rain keeps tapping the cobbles. Then, very quietly, he says: 'Ten seconds. You watch. You don't speak to her, don't touch her, don't step in if she drops her keys. You don't warn her about anything. Ten seconds, and then we leave, and she never knows you were there.' A pause. 'Can you do that?'

input: "I can do that." I say it too fast, the way you agree to anything when you're afraid the offer will be taken back. Then, slower, meaning it: "Ten seconds. I watch. I don't touch, I don't speak, I don't step in. I promise." I make myself hold his eyes when I say the word promise, because I can tell it matters to him more than the rest. "Take me there."
prose: The word promise lands between us. I see it hit — something in his face shifts, the stillness deepening, the hand on the copper bar going quiet. He doesn't smile. He just nods once, sharp, and turns back to the console. His fingers find the levers. The TARDIS's pitch climbs, a long rising note like a held breath about to break. The central column pistons faster. Through the open doors, the wet alley and the orange streetlamp are still there — then they're a smear, then they're gone, replaced by a cold grey light that hasn't decided if it's day or dusk yet. The engines groan into silence. The Doctor stands with his back to me, hands flat on the console, head bowed for a count of two. Then he turns, and his eyes are clear and hard and sad all at once. "Bethnal Green Road. 12 November 2003. Ten seconds. I'll count them."

input: I step out first, before I can lose my nerve. I want to see where I am with my own eyes.
prose: I step through the doors before the hum can talk me out of it. The golden light spills around me, warm against the damp chill, and the soles of my boots find wet cobbles. The smell of frying oil and wet cardboard hits me — real, solid, the world outside the ship. Behind me, the alley mouth opens onto Bute Street: orange streetlights, the hiss of tyres on wet asphalt. I turn at the sound of his voice. He's standing at the threshold of the TARDIS, one hand resting on the frame. He hasn't stepped out. His weight is held back, half-inside the ship. His eyes are fixed on me, utterly still. Quiet and precise: "One."

input: I look for her. I don't know what she was wearing that day, I was six, but I'd know her — I've stared at those photographs my whole life. I scan the pavement, the bus stop, the shopfronts, looking for my mum's face on a living person walking down a street she died on.
prose: I don't need to scan. I already know where she is — the beige coat, the ponytail, the white Sainsbury's bag, thirty metres east up the north side of the road. My eyes find her and stick. There. Alive. Walking. Breathing. I'm not looking at a photograph anymore. I'm looking at a woman who doesn't know she's going to die on this street, and I'm not supposed to tell her. Behind me, the Doctor says, flat and quiet: 'Two.'

input: I forget the count. I forget the Doctor, the ship, the rule, all of it — there's just her, thirty metres away, my mum, alive and ordinary and swinging a carrier bag. She stops at the kerb by the zebra crossing. Checks her watch. And I'm drinking her in, every second of the ten I'm allowed, when I see it: down the road behind her, a dark hatchback coming too fast in the wet, and she's already stepping off the kerb without looking, the way you do on a street you've walked a thousand times. I know this street. I know this moment. This is it. This is the ten seconds. My whole body goes cold and my legs want to move on their own.
prose: I forget the count. I drink her in — the beige coat, the ponytail, the white Sainsbury's bag swinging loose from her hand. She's thirty metres away and she's alive and ordinary and checking her watch at the zebra crossing the way she's done a thousand times. The street is wet. The newsagent's Evening Standard racks are still out. The lamp glow catches the rain. And then I see it. Down the road behind her, a dark hatchback coming too fast, tyres hissing on the wet, and she's already stepping off the kerb without looking. My whole body goes cold. My legs want to move on their own but they won't. I know this street. I know this moment. This is it. This is the ten seconds. The Doctor's voice reaches me from the doorway, flat and precise: "Three." His jaw is tight, the muscles visible under the streetlight. He's watching me, not the street. But my eyes are on her. The car is closing. She doesn't see it. And I can't warn her.

input: My legs move. The promise, the rule, the Doctor's voice — all of it burns away in a single white instant, and I'm running, sprinting off the kerb into the road with everything I have. The car horn blares. I don't stop. I hit my mum at a dead run, both arms around her, and I throw us both — shove her back toward the pavement, twisting so my body's between her and the car. Tyres scream on wet tarmac. I feel the wind of it pass, close enough to snatch at my coat, and then the hatchback is swerving, mounting the far kerb, and it's past us. It's past. She's on the ground under me, winded, alive, staring up at a stranger who just knocked her flat. Karen Marsh is alive on the twelfth of November 2003, and she was never supposed to be.
prose: I push up onto my elbows. The tarmac is wet through the knees of my jeans. Under me, she gasps — a raw, choked sound, her chest heaving against my ribs. Alive. The milk carton has stopped rolling. The driver's door hangs open. His voice shakes across the bonnet: "I didn't — she just stepped out —" Then the Doctor's shout rips through the wet air: "ELLIE!" I turn my head. He's already halfway across the road, coat flaring, that quiet stillness he wore at the threshold shattered into a dead sprint. The door frame he gripped is empty behind him. He's closing the distance, white plimsolls slapping wet tarmac, and for a second I see his face — not angry, not calm, something else entirely, something I can't name.

input: I get off her. I help my mum sit up — she's winded, clutching her chest, staring at me like I'm mad, and I can't speak, I can't say a single word to her, so I just make sure she's up and I back away a step. Then I turn to the Doctor as he reaches us, and I search his face, because whatever I just did, he knows what it is and I don't. "She's alive," I say, and it comes out like a question, like a plea, like I already know from his face that something is very wrong. "Doctor. She's alive. That's good. Tell me that's good." I need him to tell me it's good. And I already know he won't.
prose: I shift off her, the wet pavement cold through my knees, and take her arm, her shoulder, guide her upright. She gasps, one hand pressed to her chest, staring at me like I've grown a second head. I can't speak to her. I just make sure she's sitting, then I back away a step. The distance feels necessary. I turn to face him. He's standing in the amber spill of the TARDIS doorway, silhouetted, still. His eyes flick up to the streetlights for a half-second — a check — then snap back to me. He exhales slow through his nose. Then he says it., quiet and gentle, "Ellie." He steps backward through the doorway, one hand gripping the door edge, pulling it wider. The amber light spills further onto the wet pavement, illuminating the damp concrete, the kerb, Karen on the ground. He says it., "The lights. Look at the lights. Inside — both of you. Now." Karen manages a breath: "What... what happened? Who are you?" I search his face. I need the answer before he opens his mouth. I already know it won't be the one I want. The words come out like a question, like I'm already bracing for the fall.
